content.title: World Baseball Classic MVP | Baseball Almanac
content.text: WORLD BASEBALL CLASSIC MOST VALUABLE PLAYER AWARD The World Baseball Classic (WBC) emerged in 2006 as Major League Baseball's most ambitious attempt to create a truly global championship—one that could stand alongside the World Cup in soccer and the World Championships long overseen by the International Baseball Federation. Prior to the WBC, international baseball's major stages were fragmented: Olympic baseball (1992, 1996, 2000, 2004, 2008, and 2020) and the long-running Baseball World Cup (discontinued after 2011) drew passionate followings but rarely featured the sport's top professional talent. The WBC changed that dynamic immediately. Backed by MLB, the MLBPA, and federations around the world, it became the first tournament in which nations could field full-strength rosters of major leaguers, rising prospects, and elite professionals from Asia, Latin America, and beyond. From its inaugural edition, the Classic established itself as a showcase of national pride and high-pressure baseball. Japan's back-to-back championships in 2006 and 2009 set the early standard, while the Dominican Republic's undefeated run in 2013 and the United States' breakthrough title in 2017 demonstrated how quickly the competitive landscape could shift. By 2023, the WBC had grown into one of the most-watched baseball events on the planet, drawing massive global audiences and producing moments—such as Shohei Ohtani striking out Mike Trout for the final out—that instantly entered the sport's international canon. Within this expanding history, the World Baseball Classic Most Valuable Player Award has become one of the tournament's defining honors. Unlike MLB's season-long MVP, the WBC version recognizes a player whose performance elevates an entire nation's hopes over a concentrated, pressure-filled slate of games. Daisuke Matsuzaka set the tone by winning the first two MVP awards, anchoring Japan's early dominance with unmatched consistency on the mound. Robinson Canó became the first position player to claim the honor in 2013, powering the Dominican Republic's perfect run. Marcus Stroman's brilliance in 2017 helped deliver the United States its first title, and Shohei Ohtani's two-way heroics in 2023 produced one of the most complete tournament performances ever recorded. As the Classic continues to evolve, the WBC MVP Award stands as a record of the players who not only excelled individually, but who shaped the global narrative of baseball’s most international stage. Research by Baseball Almanac. "It's not something that everybody can experience, and it's not something that everybody can earn. So I feel that I'm very lucky. I'm really thankful about the MVP. I didn't think that it was going to be me at all. I felt that I was lucky, and I felt that it couldn't be compared to Mr. [Hisashi] Iwakuma, who pitched today. So I felt that Iwakuma would get the MVP myself." - Matsuzaka, Daisuke. Post Game Press Conference. 24 March 2009. In 2006, Daisuke Matsuzaka became the first player in baseball history to win a World Baseball Classic Most Valuable Player Award. Three years later, Dice-K posted a 3-0 record with a 2.45 ERA in the 2009 World Baseball Classic, winning all three of his starts, including a victory over the United States during the semifinals. After that performance, he became the first, and through today, only two-time recipient of a WBC MVP Award. Did you know that Robinson Cano was the first position player to win a World Baseball Classic MVP? The Dominican second baseman hit .469 with two home runs and six RBI over the course of the 2013 World Baseball Classic. Shohei Ohtani "only" hit one home run during the 2023 World Baseball Classic, but his hitting statistics; .435 batting average, four doubles, eight RBIs, ten walks, AND pitching statistics; 11 strikeouts across 9.2 innings, 2 wins, 1 save, and a 1.86 made the two-way superstar an easy choice.
